statement: In adults in Ontario, Canada, who were dispensed opioid painkillers through the public drug plan (non-cancer pain; mostly under 65 and on low incomes; 1997–2013), a gabapentin prescription in the previous 120 days was associated with higher odds of accidental opioid-related death confirmed by the coroner: gabapentin had been dispensed to 12.3% of 1,256 people who died and 6.8% of 4,619 matched controls (adjusted odds ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.18–1.88, adjusted for opioid dose, benzodiazepines, antidepressants, alcohol use disorder and other factors). By prescribed daily gabapentin dose the adjusted odds ratios were 1.32 (0.89–1.97) for low, 1.56 (1.06–2.28) for moderate and 1.58 (1.09–2.27) for high doses, with widely overlapping intervals, so a dose–response relation is not shown; anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), used as a comparison expected to carry no added risk, gave 1.14 (0.98–1.32). In people receiving methadone or buprenorphine treatment in UK general practice (1998–2014), a gabapentin or pregabalin prescription was not clearly associated with drug-poisoning death (hazard ratio 1.54, 0.60–3.98; 5 deaths) but was associated with deaths from other causes (1.83, 1.28–2.62), which suggests that the people prescribed these medicines differed in health from others. Both studies used dispensing records and did not know why gabapentin was prescribed or whether illicit drugs were used. Pregabalin with opioid painkillers has not yet been read for this answer. Whether gabapentin causes the excess deaths is not shown.
plain: Is gabapentin with opioids more dangerous? In one study in Ontario, Canada, of people getting opioid painkillers through the public drug plan, 12 in 100 people who died of an accidental opioid overdose had recently been given gabapentin, against about 7 in 100 similar people who did not die. After taking opioid dose and other medicines into account, the odds of an opioid death were about 1.5 times higher with gabapentin. Higher gabapentin doses were not clearly riskier than lower ones. A UK study of people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment found too few poisoning deaths to say, and people given gabapentin-type medicines there died more often of other causes, a sign that they were in poorer health. The studies did not know why gabapentin was prescribed or whether people used street drugs. Pregabalin with opioid painkillers is not yet covered here.
population: Ontario public-drug-plan recipients of opioid analgesics for non-cancer pain, 1997–2013 (1,256 accidental opioid-related deaths and 4,619 matched living controls; 94% under 65; 42–44% in the lowest income fifth); and, as a qualifier, 12,118 people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment in UK primary care, 1998–2014
exposure: Gabapentin dispensed in the 120 days before the index date (Ontario); a gabapentinoid (gabapentin or pregabalin) prescription during or up to 12 months after opioid agonist treatment (UK)
comparator: Opioid recipients without recent gabapentin (Ontario, matched controls); periods without a gabapentinoid prescription (UK)
outcome: Accidental opioid-related death confirmed by the coroner (Ontario); drug-poisoning and other deaths from death registrations (UK)
magnitude: Ontario (Gomes et al., 2017): recent gabapentin in 155 of 1,256 cases (12.3%) and 313 of 4,619 controls (6.8%); unadjusted OR 1.99 (95% CI 1.61–2.47), adjusted OR 1.49 (1.18–1.88); supply overlapping the date of death, adjusted OR 1.46 (1.12–1.89). By prescribed daily dose (study conditions): low (<900 mg) 41 against 101 exposed, adjusted OR 1.32 (0.89–1.97); moderate (900–1,799 mg) 57 against 111, 1.56 (1.06–2.28); high (≥1,800 mg) 57 against 101, 1.58 (1.09–2.27); post hoc ≥2,500 mg 1.83 (1.04–3.22). Negative-control exposure, NSAIDs: adjusted OR 1.14 (0.98–1.32). No absolute risks (case–control design). UK OAT (Macleod et al., 2019): gabapentinoid co-prescription, drug-poisoning deaths 5 in 538 person-years (0.93 per 100) against 108 in 19,410 (0.56), adjusted HR 1.54 (0.60–3.98); other deaths 46 in 571 (8.06 per 100) against 239 in 19,815 (1.21), adjusted HR 1.83 (1.28–2.62); all causes adjusted HR 1.71 (1.33–2.20).

evidence.locator: Abstract (Methods and findings); Results, 3rd paragraph; Fig 2 (forest plot)
evidence.extracted: Gabapentin dispensed in the prior 120 days: 155 of 1,256 cases (12.3%) and 313 of 4,619 controls (6.8%); conditional OR 1.99 (95% CI 1.61–2.47); adjusted OR 1.49 (1.18–1.88), p < 0.001, adjusted for opioid dose, age, pregabalin, SSRIs, other antidepressants, benzodiazepines, other CNS depressants, methadone or buprenorphine, number of drugs, long-acting opioid, alcohol use disorder, Charlson index, lung disease, diabetes and numbers of opioid prescribers and pharmacies. Supply overlapping the index date: 121 (9.6%) and 240 (5.2%), adjusted OR 1.46 (1.12–1.89).

evidence.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Fig 2 (forest plot); Discussion, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: By prescribed daily gabapentin dose against none: low (<900 mg) 41 cases (3.3%) and 101 controls (2.2%), adjusted OR 1.32 (0.89–1.97; the text prints 0.89–1.96); moderate (900–1,799 mg) 57 (4.5%) and 111 (2.4%), 1.56 (1.06–2.28); high (≥1,800 mg) 57 (4.5%) and 101 (2.2%), 1.58 (1.09–2.27); post hoc ≥2,500 mg, 1.83 (1.04–3.22). The authors say the intervals overlap considerably and the suggestion of a gradient should be read with caution.

evidence.locator: Methods › Exposure definition, 1st paragraph; Results, 5th paragraph; Fig 2
evidence.extracted: Prespecified negative-control exposure, NSAIDs in the prior 120 days (not expected to raise the risk of opioid-related death): 480 cases (38.2%) and 1,647 controls (35.7%); OR 1.11 (0.98–1.27), adjusted OR 1.14 (0.98–1.32), p = 0.083.

evidence.locator: Methods › Setting, 1st paragraph; Data sources, 1st paragraph; Identification of patients and outcomes, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
evidence.extracted: Ontario Public Drug Programs (people aged 65 or over, unemployed, on disability benefits, with high drug costs relative to income, in home care or long-term care), 1997–2013; opioid recipients aged 15–105 without cancer or recent palliative care. Cases: coroner-confirmed opioid-related deaths (autopsy and toxicology), suicides and homicides excluded; 1,256 of 1,391 eligible cases matched by incidence density sampling to 4,619 controls on a disease risk index, age, sex, year and kidney disease. 94.5% of cases and 94.2% of controls were under 65; 42.1% and 43.8% in the lowest income fifth; 24 cases (1.9%) also had heroin on toxicology.

The authors read the result as a drug–drug interaction and list limitations: a low-income public-plan population, mostly under 65; only government-reimbursed retail prescriptions; adherence and cash or illicit purchases unknown; the indication for gabapentin unknown; confounding by indication possible, which they argue against from the risk-index matching, opioid-dose adjustment, adjustment for severity markers and the NSAID result.
evidence.quote: support the existence of a life-threatening drug–drug interaction

evidence.locator: Abstract (Methods and findings); Results › Z-drugs and gabapentinoids, 1st paragraph; Table 4, gabapentinoid rows
evidence.extracted: In 12,118 people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment in UK primary care, gabapentinoid co-prescription: drug-poisoning deaths 5 in 538 person-years (0.93 per 100) against 108 in 19,410 (0.56), adjusted HR 1.54 (0.60–3.98), p = 0.373; all-cause deaths 83 in 998 person-years (8.32 per 100) against 574 in 35,129 (1.63), adjusted HR 1.71 (1.33–2.20); other deaths 46 in 571 (8.06 per 100) against 239 in 19,815 (1.21), adjusted HR 1.83 (1.28–2.62); no dose analysis possible; the authors call these analyses underpowered.

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded, a borderline judgment: the Ontario study is ROBINS-E some concerns (coroner-confirmed outcome, matching on a disease risk index, adjustment for opioid dose and other sedating medicines, a near-null negative control), with remaining concerns about the indication for gabapentin, gabapentin misuse and unmeasured drug use, which could make the true association smaller. The UK qualifier is ROBINS-E high but carries no weight in the rating.

inconsistency.note: The UK estimate for drug-poisoning death points the same way but is too imprecise to test consistency, and comes from a different population.

indirectness.note: None as worded: the main finding is stated for gabapentin with opioid painkillers in a public-plan population; pregabalin is stated as not studied.

imprecision.note: The main interval (1.18–1.88) excludes no association; the dose-specific and UK estimates are imprecise and the claim says so.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with one main study.

dose_response.note: Not applied: low, moderate and high doses gave 1.32, 1.56 and 1.58 with overlapping intervals and no trend test; the very-high-dose estimate is post hoc.

grade.reasoning: One nested case–control study read in full (Ontario), observational, so it starts low; not downgraded for risk of bias (ROBINS-E some concerns on the study card; borderline, see the domain note), inconsistency, indirectness or imprecision; not upgraded. Certainty low. A strict reader who judged unmeasured gabapentin misuse and drug use an important uncontrolled confounder would downgrade once to very low; the Ontario design is nonetheless the strongest among the prescription studies read in this batch, which is why this answer is rated higher than the one on benzodiazepines, whose studies are at high risk of bias. Relation: is associated with; the authors' reading of a life-threatening drug–drug interaction is causal and goes beyond an adjusted odds ratio of 1.49 with an unclear dose pattern. Status: single study; the UK treatment cohort (gabapentin and pregabalin together) is a different population, has only 5 exposed drug-poisoning deaths and shows an excess in other deaths, so it neither replicates nor contradicts the finding.

verification.flag_note: Gomes et al. 2018 on pregabalin and opioid-related death (Ann Intern Med, 10.7326/M18-1136; DOI list item 16) has not been read and is needed before this answer covers pregabalin; Lyndon et al. 2017 (Addiction, 10.1111/add.13843) and Bharat et al. 2024 (Int J Drug Policy, 10.1016/j.drugpo.2023.104287) would add people who use illicit opioids.
